title: Karan Johar Just Bowed to Malayalam Cinema. Dharma's First Mollywood Film Is a Shape-Shifter Horror With Prithviraj and Manju Warrier.
excerpt: Odiyan: The Age of Illusion reunites the man who made Bramayugam with the most ambitious folklore tale in years — and it marks the first time Bollywood's most storied banner has knocked on Kerala's door.
body:
The poster gave nothing away and everything away at once: a round baroque frame, intricate as a temple carving, cradling the skeletal remains of a small horned creature. No faces. No tagline beyond four words — *The Age of Illusion*. And yet, by the time **Karan Johar** hit publish on Tuesday afternoon, the Malayalam film internet had already decided this was the announcement of the year.

Here is why. **Dharma Productions** — the house that gave the diaspora *Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham*, *My Name Is Khan*, the entire grammar of glossy NRI longing — is making a Malayalam film. Its first. And it is not playing it safe with a feel-good family drama. It is making a folk-horror epic about a shape-shifting demon, directed by the one filmmaker in India who has quietly become untouchable in the genre.

> "I have been a great admirer of Malayalam cinema for a long time, and have always wanted to be part of that world. The craft, the courage, the way its filmmakers trust their audiences — it is something I have watched with genuine awe." — Karan Johar

That is not a press release talking. That is a man who built an empire on Punjabi weddings and chiffon sarees admitting, in public, that the most interesting cinema in the country is being made in a language he doesn't speak. Coming from Bollywood's ultimate insider, it lands like a confession.


**Odiyan: The Age of Illusion** is directed by **Rahul Sadasivan**, and if you've been paying attention, that name alone is the headline. This is the man behind *Bhoothakaalam*, *Bramayugam* and *Diés Irae* — a clean three-for-three run of atmospheric horror so controlled it makes most Bollywood thrillers look like they were edited with a chainsaw. *Bramayugam*, shot in stark black and white with **Mammootty** as a malevolent feudal lord, was the kind of film that made critics abroad sit up and ask what exactly was happening in Kerala. Sadasivan doesn't do jump scares. He does dread. Slow, beautiful, suffocating dread.

Now he gets the biggest canvas of his career. The film is described as "an epic rooted in the folklore and cultural mythology of 19th-century Kerala" — the legend of the Odiyan, a shape-shifter whose fury descends on a powerful matriarchal household, setting off a battle between truth and illusion. The eagle-eyed have already noticed that the poster shares its font and design partner, Aesthetic Kunjamma, with *Bramayugam*, which carried its own tagline: *The Age of Madness*. Sadasivan is building a vocabulary. An age of madness, then an age of illusion. Whatever this is, it's a continuation of a singular vision.

Leading it: **Prithviraj Sukumaran** and **Manju Warrier**, two of Malayalam cinema's most commanding presences. For Warrier, there's a delicious bit of trivia — this is her *second* film called *Odiyan*, after the 2018 Mohanlal vehicle. Same title, entirely different beast. Prithviraj, who is also producing through Prithviraj Productions, framed it as something close to a duty.

> "The Odiyan is not just a myth, it is a piece of Kerala's identity, a legend that has travelled through generations and continues to hold a powerful place in our cultural consciousness." — Prithviraj Sukumaran

The producing lineup tells its own story about scale and ambition: Karan Johar, **Adar Poonawalla**, Apoorva Mehta and Supriya Menon. Vaccine billions, Bollywood's biggest banner, and Kerala's most strategic star-producer, all on one folk-horror film. This is being built to travel — reports peg it as a pan-India release in Hindi, Telugu, Tamil and Kannada alongside the Malayalam original.

And that is exactly why it matters to anyone watching from Jersey City or Toronto or Wembley. The diaspora has spent the last few years quietly discovering Malayalam cinema through subtitles on streaming — *Bramayugam*, *Manjummel Boys*, *Aavesham* — and finding it richer, stranger and braver than the Hindi mainstream. Now the establishment is following the audience south. When the most commercially calculating producer in Hindi cinema decides the smart money is on a Kerala shape-shifter, the center of gravity has officially shifted.

No release date yet. No first look beyond that haunting little skeleton in its golden frame. But make no mistake: when Karan Johar starts learning Malayalam, the rest of Bollywood is about to start taking notes.
